---
title: Diagnosing a fit
jupyter: python3
---

`sim.fit()` always returns values. Whether to trust them is a separate question, with several parts: does the model match the data, did the search find the best values, are the values determined by the data, and would the fitted model predict data it hasn't seen? This page goes through the checks, in the order worth making them. It assumes the basics of [Calibration](calibration_fitting.qmd).

The examples use a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000, 90% of whom are immune. The data are a year of weekly reported cases, made from the model with a latent period of 10 days (an SEIR model), `beta = 1.9`, and half of all cases reported:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

def make_seir():
    """ Measles with a latent period: infected (E), then infectious (I) about 10 days later """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])
    report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])
    onset  = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    cases  = ss.outcome(report*onset)
    return ss.Disease(S >> E @ beta*I, onset, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9), name='measles')

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
truth = ss.Sim(make_seir(), pars=dict(beta=1.9, report=0.5), rand_seed=2, verbose=0, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_data('cases', resample='week')
```

## Does the model match the data?

Start by looking. A fit can converge perfectly and still be wrong, if the model can't produce the pattern in the data. Here the data are fitted with a model that leaves out the latent period, an SIR model:

```{python}
def make_sir():
    """ Measles without a latent period: infectious as soon as infected """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])
    report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    cases     = ss.outcome(report*infection)
    return ss.Disease(infection, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9), name='measles')

sir_fit = ss.Sim(make_sir(), data=data, **pars).fit()
```

The search converged, but the share reported ended at its upper bound of 1 (with an `AtBound` warning). Comparing the model's weekly cases with the data, and the difference between them (the residuals), shows why:

```{python}
def weekly_check(fit, data):
    """ The model's weekly cases against the data, and the residuals """
    model = fit.sim.results.measles.cases.resample('week')
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(7, 6))
    ax1.plot(data.date, model.values, label='Model')
    ax1.scatter(data.date, data.cases, color='k', s=15, label='Data')
    ax1.set_ylabel('Weekly cases')
    ax1.legend(frameon=False)
    ax2.bar(data.date, data.cases - model.values, width=5)
    ax2.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.5)
    ax2.set_ylabel('Data minus model')
    return fig

weekly_check(sir_fit, data);
```

Without a latent period, an epidemic with the same R0 grows much faster, so the SIR model can't be both as late and as large as the data: it peaks too early and too low, even with every case reported. The residuals have a pattern: too many cases in the model early on, then too few through the peak. Residuals that wander above and below zero at random, as for the right model below, are what a good fit looks like:

```{python}
seir_fit = ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, **pars).fit(verbose=False)
weekly_check(seir_fit, data);
```

A pattern in the residuals points to the structure of the model, not to the fitting: no search will fix it. The fit's measure (`fit.mismatch`) helps compare fits to the same data, here 0.38 for the SIR model against 0.10 for the SEIR model, but the plot shows *where* a model fails.

::: {.callout-warning}
## [PROPOSAL]
This check should be built in: `fit.plot()` should show the model over the data's own periods (here, weekly totals, not daily cases), and `fit.plot(residuals=True)` should add the residuals. Today `fit.plot()` plots daily cases against weekly data, and the residuals have to be worked out by hand, as above. (P11, P15)
:::

## Did the search converge?

Every fit says whether it converged, and how it decided, in `fit.converged` and `fit.why`, which are also printed:

```{python}
print(seir_fit.converged)
print(seir_fit.why)
```

What "converged" means depends on the method:

| Method | Converged when | If not |
|---|---|---|
| SciPy optimizers (`'nelder-mead'`, `'l-bfgs-b'`) | The searches from the best few starting points of a scan end at the same value | More starting points (`scan=`) or searches (`restarts=`); a sign of several local optima, or a ridge |
| Optuna | The best score improved by less than 1% over the last quarter of the trials | More trials (`trials=`) |
| NUTS, particle MCMC | The chains agree (R-hat at most 1.01) and no draws diverged | More warm-up (`warmup=`); check identifiability |
| Iterated filtering (`'if2'`) | Chains from different starts end within 2 of the best log-likelihood | More iterations or particles |

A fit that has not converged is not necessarily wrong, but it can't be trusted until it has been run longer, or until the reason it didn't is understood.

## Is a best value at a bound?

A best value at the edge of its bounds triggers an `AtBound` warning, as for the SIR model above. It means one of three things:

- The true value is beyond the bound: widen it, if larger (or smaller) values are plausible.
- The data don't determine the parameter, so nothing stops it drifting to the edge (see [Parameter identification](calibration_identification.qmd)).
- The model is missing something, and the parameter is being pushed to the edge to make up for it, as the reporting share was above. Widening its bounds to allow more than 100% of cases to be reported would make the fit better and the model worse.

## Does the fit give the same answer again?

A stochastic model is fitted to noisy scores, so a second fit, with another `rand_seed=`, shows how much the answer depends on chance. Here the model is run as a chain binomial (a stochastic compartmental model), and fitted twice:

```{python}
import pandas as pd

stochastic = ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, solver='binomial', **pars)
rows = []
for seed in [1, 4]:
    fit = stochastic.fit(trials=100, rand_seed=seed, verbose=False)
    rows.append(dict(rand_seed=seed, beta=fit.pars.beta, report=fit.pars.report, converged=fit.converged))
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)
```

β is much the same in the two fits, but the share reported is not (0.42 and 0.26, against a true 0.5), even though the second fit says it converged: convergence means the search stopped improving, not that the answer is precise. The noise in the scores is large compared with the difference that `report` makes to them. More trials, or more runs for each trial (`n_runs=`, 4 by default for a stochastic compartmental model), reduce this; so does a likelihood, which weighs the data by how much they vary. The fit also reruns its best values with the same seeds as the search, and warns when they then score worse than the starting values: the best trial may have been a lucky run.

For a stochastic model, also check the fit against many runs, not one: `fit.sim.run(n_runs=20)`, as in [Calibration](calibration_fitting.qmd#a-stochastic-model). The data should lie within the range of the runs about as often as the interval says.

## Can the data tell the parameters apart?

Starsim notes when two parameters can't be told apart (`ss.errors.Unidentifiable`): when they appear in the model only multiplied together, or (for a posterior) when they are almost perfectly correlated. Even without a note, check that the fit can recover known values from data made by the model itself, as this page's examples do. [Parameter identification](calibration_identification.qmd) covers this in detail.

## Is the posterior reliable?

For a posterior (`method='nuts'`, `'pmcmc'`, or `'abc-smc'`), `fit.summarize()` prints a table with the posterior's median and 95% interval for each parameter, and two checks for each:

- **R-hat** (`rhat`): compares the spread within each chain with the spread between chains. Near 1 means the chains have found the same distribution; above 1.01, they disagree, and the posterior is not yet reliable.
- **Effective sample size** (`ess`): how many independent draws the correlated draws are worth. A few hundred is enough for a median and a 95% interval.

NUTS also counts **divergent** draws (`fit.diagnostics.divergences`), where the sampler's path went wrong in a region of sharp curvature; even a few mean the posterior may be missing a region. If any of these checks fail, the fit warns (`ss.errors.NotConverged`). More warm-up (`warmup=`) sometimes fixes it, but a common cause is a ridge, where the data determine only a combination of parameters: then fix one, or get more data. An example of a posterior with a ridge is in [Parameter identification](calibration_identification.qmd).

## Does the model predict?

A model with more parameters usually fits better, without necessarily being better. A fairer test is how well a model fitted to the start of the data predicts the rest. `ss.fit.compare_models()` fits each model to all but the last 25% of each data series (`holdout=`), runs it forward, and scores it on the part held out:

```{python}
comparison = ss.fit.compare_models({'SIR': ss.Sim(make_sir(), data=data, **pars),
                                    'SEIR': ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, **pars)},
                                   method='nelder-mead')
comparison.summarize();
```

The SEIR model fits better and predicts better. `folds=` repeats the comparison over several cut points, which shows whether the difference is larger than the spread from one cut point to another; `comparison.plot()` shows each model's fit and prediction against the data.

## A checklist

| Check | How | A problem looks like |
|---|---|---|
| The model matches the data | Plot the model against the data, on the data's own periods, and the residuals | A pattern in the residuals; a parameter pushed to a bound |
| The search converged | `fit.converged`, `fit.why` | "Not converged", with the reason |
| No value is at a bound | The `AtBound` warning | A best value at the edge |
| The answer is stable | Fit again with another `rand_seed=` (stochastic) or from other starting points (`scan=`) | Different values each time |
| The parameters are identifiable | The `Unidentifiable` note; recover known values | A ridge, or values that move together |
| The posterior is reliable | `rhat`, `ess`, divergences | R-hat above 1.01, few effective draws, any divergences |
| The model predicts | `ss.fit.compare_models()` | A model that fits well but predicts badly |
| The fit is plausible | Compare the values with what is known from elsewhere | A reporting share above 1, an infectious period of months |

The last check matters most, and no software can make it: a fit only finds the values that make this model match these data. Whether those values, and the model, make sense for the disease and the setting is a judgment for the modeler.
